papers.title: Pricing with bandits in the long tail: The role of competitive monitoring
EXPRESS: Infinite-Scrolling vs. Pagination: The Impact of Interface Layouts on Product Returns
papers.authors: Huitian Zhang, Lei Su, Jaideep Sengupta
papers.abstract: Interface layout, although a fundamental and prominent aspect inherent to online interfaces, has received limited attention in consumer research. This paper explores how the two major types of interface layout (infinite scrolling and pagination) influence consumers’ product return behavior in the context of free returns, a standard policy on e-commerce sites. Across five studies featuring real websites, we show that an infinite-scrolling (versus paginated) layout increases consumers’ tendency to return purchased products. This effect occurs because infinite scrolling dampens consumers’ perceived navigational control over the website, which impairs their choice closure after making decisions, thereby increasing product return intentions. We also identify both theoretically relevant and managerially important moderators and interventions to mitigate this adverse effect of infinite scrolling, such as incorporating navigational aids (e.g., displaying sequence numbers alongside), providing affirmative feedback, and accounting for the cost of product returns. This research not only contributes to the literature on interface effects, website navigation, and product returns but also provides applied insights for marketing practitioners.

papers.title: EXPRESS: The Humanizing Power of Accents in Voicebots: When Accent-Based Humanization Increases User Engagement
papers.authors: Hesam Ghasemi, Amir Sepehri, Cait Lamberton
papers.abstract: Given that consumers often exhibit resistance toward algorithmic systems, firms face challenges in encouraging engagement with voicebots. In this paper, we find that users’ engagement with voicebots may be enhanced by endowing these tools with non-standard accents that deviate from “standard” pronunciation. Across a range of accents, languages, genders, and contexts, our data suggest that voicebots communicating with non-standard accents make the concept of human diversity salient in the users’ minds. As a result, voicebots communicating with non-standard accents are more readily anthropomorphized. This effect translates into greater preference for the non-standard accented voicebot in customer service settings, stronger support for startups leveraging accented vs. unaccented voicebots, higher willingness to pay for monthly subscriptions, and a greater likelihood of opting in to receive future updates and communications. Consistent with our theory, however, these effects do not hold when the anthropomorphism effect is either overridden by other cues or is undesirable for the consumer. Together, this work highlights the benefits of accented speech in improving human-AI interactions. We also hope that it sparks further investigation into factors that make technology more readily accepted by consumers.

papers.title: Returnless Partial Refunds: A Large-Scale Field Experiment in E-Commerce
papers.authors: Lu Fang, Chunhua Wu, Zhe Yuan, Kaifu Zhang
papers.abstract: A large-scale field experiment shows AI-enabled returnless partial refunds increase customer value and reduce operating costs while raising strategic-behavior risks.

papers.title: Thank You, Now What? How Donors Respond to Calls to Action
papers.authors: K. Sudhir, Hortense Fong, Yonat Zwebner, Subroto Roy
papers.abstract: We study whether thank-you communications charities send to past donors should include a call to action (CTA), a direct request to give again, and show that the answer depends on whether the donor has already given in the current giving cycle. Although CTAs can clarify desired behavior and increase compliance, they may backfire when the request asks for giving beyond a donor’s typical cadence and violates expectations about when requests are appropriate. In a field experiment with 35,077 prior donors to a major Indian charity, we compare thank-you letters that include a CTA with otherwise identical letters without one. Response rates are low, as is typical in direct mail, with 0.69% of recipients giving. The CTA x recency interaction is statistically significant for donation amounts. Among donors who have not yet given in the current cycle, the CTA significantly increases giving, whereas among donors who have already given, point estimates indicate lower giving. The CTA helps one segment but is associated with lower giving in the other, so aggregate evaluations mask this heterogeneity. The results suggest that a donor’s giving status within the current cycle, a simple observable characteristic, can improve the targeting of fundraising communications and meaningfully affect revenue.
